summary: Ten mutations run individually in an isolated copy of the staged bytes; the tests are strong and every claim their comments make about which mutant they kill was verified true rather than taken at face value. Killed: filter deleted at BOTH sites (all 4 tests fail); deleted at chainEnd ONLY (tests 3+4 fail, 1+2 pass); deleted at applyChain ONLY (tests 1+2+3 fail, 4 passes) -- so the two listing sites are independently pinned, which is the criterion an earlier draft of this row warned could be faked; `break` for skip at chainEnd (killed by findingTheChainEnd..., and ONLY by it); `return` for skip at applyChain (killed by recoveryIgnoresKeys..., at the nextSequence assertion, line 127); deny-list `!endsWith(".ckpt")`; `contains(".delta")`; `return true`; and the SWALLOWING form (no key filter, `catch (IOException) { continue; }` around the read) which is killed by the GET-count test AND by CommitLogTest.recoveryStopsOnAnEntryItCannotUnderstandRatherThanSkippingIt, verified by mutation. Bare `endsWith(SUFFIX)` survives tests 1, 2 and 4 and is killed ONLY by aValidEntryAtAKeyThisLogNeverWroteIsNotPartOfItsChain -- the comment's claim, confirmed. Fixture claims verified by measurement, not argument: the alien body's sequence really is 9 (asserted temporarily against decode(alien).sequence(), passed); deleting seedInterposed from the chain-end test makes the `break` mutant survive ALL FOUR tests, so the interposed `.delta.tmp` key is load-bearing exactly as the comment says and a trailing `ckpt/` key alone would not kill it; the GET-count test's baseline is 4 GETs, not 0, so the equality is not vacuous, and taking both counts against the same backing store is sound because recover() is read-only and each CountingBinStore is fresh; test 3's nextOffset(RA) assertion bites on its own (with both nextSequence assertions removed it still kills the endsWith mutant, 20 vs 7). No existing test file is touched by this diff, so testing.md rules 4-5 are not in play; CommitLogTest.recoveryStopsOnAnEntryItCannotUnderstandRatherThanSkippingIt passes unchanged and is NOT made vacuous by the new filter -- it seeds its corrupt entry at log.keyFor(1), a canonical key the allow-list admits, and it still fails under the swallow mutant. Tier is right (T1 over MemoryBinStore, whose ConcurrentSkipListMap gives the lexicographic order the 'sorts in the middle' fixture depends on), no sleep, no port, no system temp, no mock. Two minors, neither blocking: one measured surviving mutant on the new code, and one new method with no caller and no test. Tree restored: `git diff` empty in the review copy and `./gradlew test` BUILD SUCCESSFUL; the staged diff in the repository is untouched (sha256 fcf8d15b8ee8a3362ed2a86f45fb2b206509e7ff363f33fd31868c78a30d7d76).

findings.title: SURVIVING MUTANT, MEASURED: the canonical-regeneration half of isEntryKey is unconstrained by any test
findings.detail: The mutation: delete the final `return key.equals(keyFor(sequence));` and `return true` after the parse succeeds (keeping startsWith + endsWith + parseUnsignedLong). Result: all four new tests pass, and the FULL `./gradlew test` is BUILD SUCCESSFUL. The line is executed but not constrained -- testing.md rule 8's characteristic failure. What survives is precisely the property the class javadoc advertises as the reason for this form ('would silently admit an unpadded, uppercase, wrong-length or one-segment-deeper key that no writer can produce') and that the task row calls the design ('keyFor RUN BACKWARDS ... it IS the writer'). The one-segment-deeper case IS covered, by the parse failing on `ckpt/...`; unpadded, uppercase and over-long hex are not. Concrete failure scenario: a key such as `<logPrefix>9.delta` or `<logPrefix>000000000000000A.delta` -- a foreign tool, a future writer, or a hand-repaired object -- carrying a decodable CommitDelta would be admitted, GET, folded and would drive nextSequence past this chain's real end, silently, which is the same I2 the fourth test exists to forbid one grammar-level up. Cheapest kill is a T0 test on LogKeys itself (testing.md rule 1 prefers it, and there is currently NO direct test of LogKeys at all): assert isEntryKey rejects an unpadded and an uppercase-hex key and accepts keyFor(n). Alternatively, testing.md rule 9 is satisfied by an argued entry in a STAGED baselines/mutants.txt -- this diff neither kills it nor argues it there.
findings.failure_scenario: Delete the final `return key.equals(keyFor(sequence));` from LogKeys.isEntryKey and `return true` once the hex parses: all four new tests pass and the full `./gradlew test` is BUILD SUCCESSFUL (measured). In production that mutant admits a non-canonical key -- `<logPrefix>9.delta` (unpadded) or `<logPrefix>000000000000000A.delta` (uppercase hex) -- written by a foreign tool or a hand repair. It is GET, decoded, folded, and drives this chain's nextSequence past its real end with nothing thrown and nothing logged; the next commit is written into a slot the chain never reached, which is I2 -- exactly the failure aValidEntryAtAKeyThisLogNeverWroteIsNotPartOfItsChain forbids one grammar level up.

findings.title: New method CommitLog.isEntryKey has no caller and no test; a no-op mutation kills nothing
findings.detail: The mutation: replace the delegate body with `return false;`. Full `./gradlew test` is BUILD SUCCESSFUL. `grep -rn isEntryKey` finds only its own definition -- both call sites in ChainReplay go to LogKeys directly, and no test, fixture or simulation calls it. It is new production surface added by this commit with nothing constraining it in either direction. The other delegates (keyFor, logPrefix) are justified in the row as scope control for ten existing test files; this one has no such caller to protect. Either delete it or let the next task that needs it add it with a test. Flagged here because a reviewer looking only for weak TESTS should also report new production code that no test can distinguish from a no-op; the production reviewer may prefer to own the deletion.
findings.failure_scenario: Replace the body of CommitLog.isEntryKey with `return false;`: the full `./gradlew test` is BUILD SUCCESSFUL (measured). No caller exists (`grep -rn isEntryKey` finds only the definition and the two ChainReplay sites, which use LogKeys directly). The scenario is a later caller adopting it on the assumption it is exercised -- a wrong or inverted delegate here would reach that caller with no test able to tell it apart from a no-op, and the commit that adopts it would look covered because the method already 'existed and passed'.
